This objection was raised against him: when the governing element falls upon a predicate that has a complement, two possibilities arise. The first is negating only that complement, as in your saying "mā Zaydun bi-dhāhibin musriʿan" (Zayd is not going quickly): the quickness is negated, but not the going itself, and there is no impediment to affirming going in a manner other than quickly. The second is negating the predicate itself, so that its complement is negated along with it: going is negated in this state, and quickness is negated with it. Thus if ﴿bi-niʿmati rabbika﴾ is made a complement of ﴿majnūn﴾, one of two things follows, and both are certainly false.

This objection here is faulty, because the meaning, once established as "you are not mad, being favoured by your Lord," entails with certainty the negation of madness when this report is true, and it is not valid to negate the complement while affirming the governing element in this statement. No one endowed with the faculty of understanding grasps from it anything other than this: madness has been removed from you by God's grace upon you, and the removal from us is what this objector understood: by God's grace upon us.

Then He, glorified, informed of the perfection of His Prophet's state in both his worldly life and the Hereafter, saying: ﴿And indeed for you is a reward never cut off.﴾ That is, uninterrupted, rather continuous and enduring. The word "reward" (ajr) is indefinite for the sake of magnification, as in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson﴾, ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾, ﴿Indeed for the righteous is an achievement﴾, and ﴿And indeed for him with Us is nearness and a good return﴾, and it is frequent. The indefiniteness is for magnification because it presents to the hearer a matter of great magnitude that description cannot grasp and expression cannot attain.

This is among the greatest signs of his prophethood and messengership for whomever Allah grants understanding. The Mother of the Believers was asked about his character (ﷺ), and she answered in a way that satisfied and sufficed: "His character was the Qur'an." Her questioner understood this, so he stood up and asked her nothing further. Ibn 'Abbas and others said, in explanation of ﴿Indeed, you are of a tremendous character﴾, that it means "of a tremendous religion." Religion is called character (khuluq) because khuluq is a composite state formed from true knowledge, pure intentions, outward and inward actions that conform to justice, wisdom, and benefit, and statements that agree with the truth. These statements and actions issue from that knowledge and those intentions, so that the soul acquires through them traits that are the purest, noblest, and most excellent of traits. These were the traits of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), drawn from the niche of the Qur'an. His speech conformed to the Qur'an, explaining and clarifying it; his knowledge was the knowledge of the Qur'an; his will and actions were what the Qur'an enjoined and recommended; his aversion and abandonment were of what the Qur'an forbade; his desire was for what the Qur'an desired, his indifference to what it made indifferent, his dislike of what it disliked, and his love of what it loved; and his striving was in carrying out its commands, conveying it, and striving in its establishment. The Mother of the Believers, through her complete knowledge of the Qur'an and of the Messenger, and her excellent expression of all this in her words "His character was the Qur'an," conveyed it, and her questioner understood this meaning, so he was content and satisfied.

If the characters, knowledge, wills, and actions of people are derived from the pen and what they write, and if the creation of the pen and writing is a favor and kindness to them, since through it they reached that, then how can they deny the favor and kindness of Allah toward His servant and messenger, who was given the highest character and the most excellent knowledge, actions, and wills, whose details minds cannot reach without pen and writing? Is this not among the greatest signs of his prophethood and evidence of the truth of his messages? His enemies who denied him will know which of them is the deluded one, whether it is he or they. They and the wise already knew this in this world, their knowledge will increase in the barzakh (intermediate realm), and it will be revealed and manifested fully in the Hereafter, to the extent that the feet of all creatures will be equal in knowing it.

(A Great Benefit)
The Prophet combined the fear of Allah (taqwa) and good character, because taqwa of Allah rectifies what lies between the servant and his Lord, and good character rectifies what lies between him and his creation.
Taqwa of Allah necessitates for him the love of Allah, and good character calls to His love.

[Section: Love is the Root of Every Religion]
Just as love and will are the root of every act, as has already been mentioned, they are also the root of every religion, whether it is true or false. Religion consists of inward and outward actions, and love and will are the root of all of that. Religion is obedience, worship, and character: it is the constant, enduring obedience that has become a disposition and habit. For this reason khuluq (character) was explained as religion in Allah's saying: ﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4].
Imam Ahmad reported from Ibn 'Uyaynah that Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed, you are of a tremendous religion."
"'Aishah was asked about the character of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and she said: 'His character was the Qur'an.'"
Religion (din) carries the sense of humbling and subjugation, and also the sense of humiliation, submission, and obedience. Therefore it is used from the higher to the lower, as one says: "I subjugated him, so he submitted (dana)," meaning "I overpowered him, so he was humbled." The poet said:
"He subjugated the Rabab when they disliked religion, so they became [subdued] despite their might and dominance."
It is also used from the lower to the higher, as one says: "I worshipped Allah (dintu Allah), I submitted to Allah (dintu lillah)," and "So-and-so does not worship Allah with any religion," meaning "He does not submit to Allah with any religion." Thus "danā Allah" means he obeyed Allah, loved Him, and feared Him; and "dāna Allah" means he humbled himself before Him, was lowly, submitted, and yielded.
Inward religion necessarily involves love and humility, just as worship does, unlike outward religion, which does not necessarily entail love, although it contains outward submission and humiliation.

(Section)
Among the praiseworthy qualities of the Prophet (ﷺ) is what Allah created in him of noble traits and honorable dispositions. Whoever considers his character and dispositions (ﷺ) will know that they are the best of human characters and the most honorable of human dispositions. He (ﷺ) was the most knowledgeable of creatures, the greatest in trustworthiness, the most truthful in speech, the most forbearing, the most generous, the most bountiful, the most able to bear hardship, the greatest in pardon and forgiveness, and the increase of ignorance toward him never increased him except in forbearance.
As al-Bukhari reported in his Sahih from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said concerning the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Torah:
"Muhammad, My servant and My messenger, I have named him al-Mutawakkil (the one who relies upon Allah). He is not harsh, nor rough, nor loud in the markets, and he does not repay evil with evil, but pardons and overlooks. I will not take him until through him I have set straight the crooked nation, by their saying: 'There is no god but Allah,' and through him I will open blind eyes, deaf ears, and sealed hearts."
He was the most merciful and gentle of creatures toward them, the greatest of creatures in benefiting them in their religion and their worldly life, the most eloquent of Allah's creatures, and the best in expressing many meanings in concise words that point to the intended sense. He was the most patient in the situations requiring patience, the most truthful in situations of encounter, the most faithful to covenant and obligation, the greatest in repaying good with much more than its like, the most humble, the most self-sacrificing in preferring others over himself, and the most fiercely protective and defensive of his companions. He was the most upright in carrying out what he commanded and the most distant from what he forbade, and the most connected to his kin. He is most deserving of the words of the one who said:
"Gentle toward the near, merciful, and toward enemies, firm and unyielding."
'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the most generous of people in heart, the most truthful in speech, the gentlest in disposition, and the most noble in companionship. Whoever saw him suddenly was awed by him, and whoever associated with him knowingly loved him. His describer says: 'I have not seen anyone before him or after him like him.'" (ﷺ)

As for his saying "the most generous of people in heart" (asdaq al-nas sadran), it means the goodness of his breast, the abundance of his good, that goodness gushed forth from him abundantly, and that he embodied every beautiful trait and every good. As some scholars said: "There is no place in the whole world that contained more good than the breast of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); he gathered goodness in its entirety and deposited it in his breast (ﷺ)."

As for his saying "the most truthful of people in speech," this is something his enemies who fought him acknowledged. None of his enemies ever found him guilty of a single lie, let alone the testimony of all his allies in this regard. The people of the earth fought him with every kind of warfare, both polytheists and People of the Book, yet not one of them ever accused him of a single lie, small or great, at any time.
Al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: "I said to Abu Jahl, and he was my maternal uncle: 'O uncle, did you used to accuse Muhammad of lying before he made his claim?'
He said: 'By Allah, O nephew, Muhammad was a youth called among us al-Amin (the Trustworthy). When grey hair appeared on him, he would not have lied.'
I said: 'O uncle, then why do you not follow him?' He said: 'O nephew, we and the Banu Hashim competed for honor. They fed and we fed, they gave drink and we gave drink, they gave protection and we gave protection. When we were kneeling side by side like two horses in a race, they said: "From us is a prophet." So when will we get such a thing?' or as he said."

Allah, the Exalted, said, consoling him and making light for him the words of his enemies: ﴿We know that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah. And messengers before you were denied, but they were patient over what they were denied and harmed until Our victory came to them. And there is no changer of the words of Allah. And there has already come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾.

As for his saying "the gentlest in disposition" (alyanahum 'arikah), it means easy and gentle, near to people, responsive to the call of whoever calls him, fulfilling the need of whoever seeks his judgment, consoling the heart of whoever comes to him, not depriving him or turning him away disappointed. When his companions wanted something from him, he agreed with them and followed them in it; and if he resolved upon a matter, he did not decide it alone apart from them, but consulted them and took counsel with them. He accepted from the good among them and pardoned the wrongdoers among them.

As for his saying "the most noble in companionship" (akramuhum 'ishrah), it means that he never kept company with a companion except in the most complete and best and most honorable companionship. He never frowned in his face, never was harsh in his speech, never hid his cheerfulness from him, and did not hold against him the slips of his tongue or hold him accountable for what came from him of rudeness or the like. Rather, he was kind to his companions to the utmost degree of kindness and bore with them to the utmost degree of forbearance. So his companionship with them meant bearing their harm and rudeness altogether; he never punished any of them, never blamed him, and never confronted him with what he disliked. Whoever associated with him would say: "I am the most beloved of people to him," because of his gentleness toward him, his nearness to him, his attention to him, his concern for his affairs, his sacrifice for him, his giving of kindness to him, and his bearing of his rudeness. What companionship was or could be more honorable than this companionship?

Al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I asked my father about the conduct of the Prophet (ﷺ) with his companions. He said: 'The Prophet (ﷺ) was always cheerful, easy in disposition, gentle in manner, neither harsh nor rough, neither loud, nor foul-mouthed, nor fault-finding, nor flattering. He overlooked what he did not desire, did not disappoint the one who hoped in him, and did not deny him. He had abandoned himself of three things: disputation, excess, and what did not concern him. He did not disparage anyone, did not blame him, did not seek his faults, and did not speak except for what he hoped its reward would be. When he spoke, his companions lowered their heads as if birds were upon their heads; when he was silent, they spoke, and they did not dispute in his presence. Whoever spoke in his presence, they listened to him until he finished his speech. He laughed at what they laughed at and marveled at what they marveled at. He was patient with strangers over their rudeness in speech and questioning, until his companions would bring them in to him. He said: "When you see someone seeking a need, help him." He accepted praise only from one who would reciprocate it, and he did not cut off anyone's speech until it went beyond its proper bounds, and then he would cut it off by forbidding it or by standing up.'"

As for his saying "whoever saw him suddenly was awed by him, and whoever associated with him knowingly loved him," he described him with two qualities that Allah specifically granted to the people of truthfulness and sincerity: reverence (ijlal) and love. He had been granted awe and love. Everyone who saw him was in awe of him, honored him, and filled his heart with veneration and reverence, even if he was his enemy. But when he associated with him and kept his company, he became more beloved to him than any created being. So he was the revered, the magnified, the beloved, the honored. This is the perfection of love: that it be joined with veneration and awe. Love without awe or veneration is deficient, and awe and veneration without love are also deficient, as they are for a treacherous wrongdoer. Perfection is that love, affection, veneration, and reverence are combined. This exists only when the beloved possesses the attributes of perfection by which he deserves to be venerated and loved. Since Allah, glory be to Him, is more deserving of this than anyone, He is the one deserving to be venerated, magnified, feared, loved, and desired with every part of the heart, and no partner should be made for Him in this. This is the shirk that Allah will not forgive: to equate anything with Him in this love. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among the people are those who take other than Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah; but those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾.
So He informed that whoever loves anything other than Allah in the same way as he loves Allah has taken it as a rival. And the people of the Fire said in the Fire to their objects of worship: ﴿By Allah, we were certainly in clear error when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾.

[Section: The Station of Character]
[Character in the Book and the Sunnah]
Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of character.
Allah, the Exalted, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4].
Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "Of a tremendous religion, no religion is more beloved to me or more pleasing to me than it, and it is the religion of Islam."
Al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It is the etiquettes of the Qur'an."
Qatadah said: "It is what he used to command from the command of Allah and forbid from the prohibition of Allah."
The meaning is: indeed, you are upon the character with which Allah has favored you in the Qur'an.
In the two Sahihs: Hisham ibn Hakim asked 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) about the character of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and she said: "His character was the Qur'an." He said: "I almost resolved to stand up and not ask anything."
Allah has gathered for him the noble traits of character in His saying: ﴿Take what is easy and enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199].
Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: "Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) with the noble traits of character. There is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of noble traits than this verse." It is also mentioned that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this?" He said: "I do not know until I ask." So he asked, then returned to him and said: "Indeed Allah commands you to join the one who cuts you off, to give to the one who withholds from you, and to pardon the one who wrongs you."

There is no doubt that the one obeyed among people has three situations:
The first: commanding them and forbidding them with what is in their benefit.
The second: taking from them what they offer of the obedience incumbent upon them.
The third: that people with him are of two kinds: one who agrees with him and is loyal, and one who opposes him and stands against him. He has an obligation in each of these.
His obligation in commanding and forbidding them is to enjoin what is right, meaning what is good for them and the good of their affairs, and to forbid them from its opposite.
His obligation regarding what they offer him of obedience is to take from them what is easy for them, what their souls have willingly and freely yielded, and not to burden them into hardship and difficulty, lest he corrupt them.
His obligation when the ignorant act ignorantly toward him is to turn away from them, not to repay them in kind, and not to take revenge upon them for himself.
Allah, the Exalted, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Take what is easy, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199].
'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Allah commanded His Prophet to take what is easy from the characters of people." Mujahid said: "It means: take what is easy from people's characters and actions without humiliating them, such as accepting excuses, pardoning, being lenient, not insisting on investigating and searching for the realities of their inner selves."
Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Take what is left over of their wealth, which is the surplus beyond one's dependents." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: "The surplus"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219].
Then He said: ﴿And enjoin what is right﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], which is every good deed. The most important of it is tawhid, then the rights of worship, then the rights of people.
Then He said: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], meaning: if the ignorant person acts foolishly toward you, do not respond to him with foolishness, as in His saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say: "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63].

Thus it is not abrogated (naskh). Rather, one turns away from him while upholding God's right over him, and does not avenge oneself.

Such was the character of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Anas (may God be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the best of people in character."

He also said: "I never touched silk brocade or silk softer than the palm of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Nor did I ever smell a fragrance better than the fragrance of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). I served the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for ten years, and he never said to me, 'Uff' (a word of complaint). Nor did he ever say, regarding something I had done, 'Why did you do it?' Nor, regarding something I had not done, 'Why did you not do it?'" Agreed upon by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) also informed that righteousness (al-birr) is good character.

In Sahih Muslim, from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an (may God be pleased with him), who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about righteousness and sin. He said: 'Righteousness is good character. Sin is that which gnaws at your chest, and you dislike that people should become aware of it.'"

So he set righteousness against sin. He informed that righteousness is good character, and sin is the gnawing of the chests. This indicates that good character is the whole of religion. It is the realities of faith and the laws of Islam. For this reason he set it against sin.

In another hadith: "Righteousness is that with which the soul is at ease, and sin is that which gnaws in the chest."

Good character has been explained as righteousness. This indicates that good character is the tranquility of the soul and the heart, while sin is the gnawing of the chests, what gnaws within them, and what they feel doubt about.

This differs from good and bad character as understood by many people, as will come in the Sahihayn from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The best of you are those best in character."

In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu al-Darda' (may God be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Nothing weighs heavier in the scale of the believer on the Day of Resurrection than good character. Indeed God, exalted is He, dislikes the foul-mouthed and the obscene."

Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

Also in it, and he authenticated it, from Abu Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him): "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about what most admits people to Paradise. He said: 'The fear of God and good character.' He was asked about what most admits people to the Fire. He said: 'The mouth and the private parts.'"

Also in it, from Aisha (may God be pleased with her), from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he authenticated it: "Among the most perfect of believers in faith are those best in character. And the best of you are the best of you to their wives."

In the Sahih, from Aisha, from him (ﷺ): "Indeed the believer attains by his good character the rank of one who fasts constantly and stands in prayer at night." Narrated by Abu Dawud.

From Ibn Umar (may God be pleased with them both), from him (ﷺ): "I guarantee a house on the outskirts of Paradise for one who abandons disputation even if he is in the right; a house in the middle of Paradise for one who abandons lying even if joking; and a house in the highest part of Paradise for one whose character is good." Narrated by al-Tabarani, and its chain is sahih.

Thus he made the highest house the reward for the highest of the three stations, which is good character. The middle house is for the middle one, which is abandoning lying. The lowest house is for the lowest one, which is abandoning disputation, even if one has the right on his side. There is no doubt that good character comprises all of this.

In al-Tirmidhi, from Jabir (may God be pleased with him), from him (ﷺ): "Indeed, among you the most beloved to me and the closest to me in sitting on the Day of Resurrection are those best in character. And indeed, among you the most hateful to me and the farthest from me on the Day of Resurrection are the verbose (al-tharthaarun), the affectedly eloquent (al-mutashaddiqun), and the bombastic (al-mutafayhiqun)."

They said: "O Messenger of God, we know the verbose and the affectedly eloquent. What are the bombastic?" He said: "The arrogant."

Al-tharthar: one who talks much without any religious benefit.

Al-mutashaddiq: one who speaks with his mouth full, showing eloquence, self-importance, and arrogance, displaying his superiority over others. Its root is from al-fahq, which is fullness.

[Section: The whole of religion is character]

The whole of religion is character. Whoever surpasses you in character surpasses you in religion. Likewise, Sufism (al-tasawwuf, mysticism).

Al-Kinani said: "Sufism is character. Whoever surpasses you in character has surpassed you in Sufism."

It has been said: good character is giving generously, withholding harm, and bearing harm.

It has been said: good character is giving what is good and withholding what is bad.

It has been said: it is emptying oneself of vices and adorning oneself with virtues.

Good character stands upon four pillars, and its shaft cannot be conceived as standing except upon them: patience (al-sabr), chastity (al-iffah), courage (al-shajaah), and justice (al-adl).

Patience compels one to forbearance, swallowing anger, withholding harm, clemency, deliberation, gentleness, and avoiding recklessness and haste.

Chastity compels one to avoid vices and ugliness in speech and action, and compels one to modesty (al-haya'), which is the head of all good. It prevents one from indecency, miserliness, lying, backbiting, and slander.

Courage compels one to self-respect, to preferring the lofty qualities and noble traits, and to giving and generosity, which is the courage of the soul and its strength to release what is loved and part with it. It compels one to swallow anger and to forbearance.

For by the strength and courage of his soul he holds its reins and restrains it with its bridle from provocation and aggression, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The strong one is not the one who overthrows people, but the strong one is the one who controls himself at the time of anger." This is the reality of courage, and it is a faculty by which the servant prevails over his opponent.

Justice compels one to balance one's character and to moderation within it, between the two extremes of excess and deficiency. It compels one to the character of generosity and liberality, which is a mean between servility and shamelessness; and to the character of courage, which is a mean between cowardice and recklessness; and to the character of forbearance, which is a mean between anger and humiliation and the collapse of the soul.

The source of all praiseworthy characters is these four.

The source of all base characters, and their construction, rests upon four pillars: ignorance, injustice, desire, and anger.

Ignorance shows him the good in the form of the bad, and the bad in the form of the good, and perfection as deficiency and deficiency as perfection.

Injustice compels him to place a thing in other than its proper place. So he becomes angry in a place of contentment, content in a place of anger, ignorant in a place of deliberation, miserly in a place of giving, giving in a place of miserliness, holds back in a place of advance, advances in a place of holding back, is soft in a place of firmness, is firm in a place of softness, is humble in a place of dignity, and is proud in a place of humility.

Desire compels him to greed, avarice, miserliness, lack of chastity, gluttony, covetousness, humiliation, and all lowly matters.

Anger compels him to arrogance, rancor, envy, aggression, and foolishness.

Between every two of these characters there is composed a number of blameworthy characters.

The essence of these four is two roots: the soul's excess in weakness, and its excess in strength. From the soul's excess in weakness arise humiliation and miserliness, baseness and meanness, servility and greed, avarice and the lowest matters and characters.

From its excess in strength arise injustice, anger, hastiness, foul speech, and recklessness.

From the marriage of one of these two characters with the other arise many illegitimate offspring. For the soul may combine strength and weakness, so its possessor becomes the most coercive of people when able, and the most humiliated when overcome: a tyrant, oppressive and domineering. But when he is overcome he becomes more abject than a woman: a coward before the strong and bold against the weak.

Thus blameworthy characters beget one another, just as praiseworthy characters beget one another.

Every praiseworthy character is flanked by two blameworthy characters, and it is a mean between them. Its two extremes are blameworthy characters, such as generosity, which is flanked by the characters of miserliness and wastefulness; and humility, which is flanked by the characters of servility and abasement; and by pride and haughtiness.

When the soul deviates from moderation, it inevitably deviates toward one of the two blameworthy characters. When it deviates from humility, it deviates either into pride and haughtiness, or into servility, abasement, and degradation. When it deviates from modesty, it deviates either into shamelessness and boldness, or into weakness, feebleness, and abasement, to the point that its enemy becomes greedy for it, and it loses much of its interests. It thinks that what drives it to this is modesty, when in fact it is abasement, weakness, and the death of the soul.

Likewise, when it deviates from the praiseworthy character of patience, it deviates either into impatience, panic, greed, and discontent, or into hardness of heart, harshness of liver, and stony disposition. As one of them said:

"You weep over us, but we do not weep over anyone, for we are harder of liver than camels."

When it deviates from the character of forbearance, it deviates either into recklessness, luxury, hastiness, and levity, or into humiliation, abasement, and baseness. So there is a difference between one whose forbearance is the forbearance of humiliation, abasement, baseness, and weakness, and one whose forbearance is the forbearance of power, dignity, and nobility. As it has been said:

"Every forbearance that comes without power
is a proof to which the base take refuge."

When it deviates from the character of deliberation and gentleness, it deviates either into haste, recklessness, and violence, or into negligence and waste. Gentleness and deliberation lie between them.

When it deviates from the character of dignity which God granted to the believers, it deviates either into pride or into abasement. Praiseworthy dignity lies between them.

When it deviates from the character of courage, it deviates either into reckless and unpraiseworthy rashness, or into cowardice and blameworthy hanging back.

When it deviates from the character of competing for high ranks and noble envy (al-ghibtah), it deviates either into envy, or into humiliation, weakness, abasement, and contentment with the lowly.

When it deviates from contentment, it deviates either into greed and voracity, or into baseness, humiliation, and waste.

When it deviates from the character of mercy, it deviates either into harshness, or into weakness of heart and cowardice of soul, like one who does not advance to slaughter a sheep, nor to carry out a legal punishment, nor to discipline a child, and claims that mercy compels him to that. Yet the most merciful of creation (ﷺ) slaughtered with his own hand, on one occasion, sixty-three camels. He cut off the hands of men and women, struck necks, carried out the prescribed punishments, and stoned the adulterer with stones until the one stoned died. And he was the most merciful and compassionate of God's creatures, without qualification.

Likewise, cheerfulness of countenance and praiseworthy good cheer. For it is a mean between frowning, scowling, turning away the cheek, and concealing cheer from people, and between indulging in that with everyone, to the point that it removes awe, dispels dignity, and invites greed. Just as the first deviation produces estrangement, hatred, and aversion in the hearts of people.

The person of moderate character is awe-inspiring and beloved, his side is honored, and his company is sweet. In the description of our Prophet (ﷺ), whoever saw him suddenly stood in awe of him, and whoever mixed with him for a while loved him. And God knows best.

[Section: Changing the characters upon which souls were formed]

This is extremely beneficial and of great benefit to the wayfarer. It brings him soon to his goal and moves him along by means of his characters, which he cannot remove. For the most difficult thing for human nature is changing the characters upon which souls were formed. Those who practised difficult spiritual disciplines (riyada) and arduous struggles worked upon these, but most of them did not succeed in transforming them. But the soul was occupied with those disciplines away from the manifestation of its dominion. When the dominion of those characters comes and emerges, it breaks the armies of discipline and scatters them, and takes control of the kingdom of nature.

This is a section by which the wayfarer connects with those characters, and does not need to treat them or remove them. His journey will be stronger, more majestic, and swifter than the journey of one who labours to remove them.

Before this, we shall present an example we strike, matching what we intend. It is: a river flowing in its descent and its slope, ending in the flooding of land, habitations, and homes. Its people know that it will not stop until it ruins their houses, destroys their lands and their wealth. They divided into three groups.

One group directed their strength and the strength of their efforts toward damming it, imprisoning it, and halting it. This group achieves nothing great, for it is about to gather strength, then rise up to overflow, and its destruction and ruin will be greater.

A group saw this condition and knew that the spring's (river's) water would not benefit them at all. They said: "There is no escape from its harm except by cutting it off at the root of the spring." So they tried to cut it off at its source. But that proved utterly impossible for them, and the nature of the river refused this most strongly. So they are always busy cutting off the spring, and whenever they block it at one point, it gushes forth at another. These people thus occupied themselves with the matter of this river and neglected cultivation, construction, and planting trees.

Then a third group came, which opposed the opinion of the two groups. They knew that much of their benefit had been lost to them. So they set about diverting that river from its course, which led to inhabited land, and they redirected it to a place where they could benefit from its arrival without being harmed by it. They diverted it to land suitable for plant growth and irrigated it with it. It produced all kinds of grass, herbage, and fruits of different varieties. So this group was the most correct of the groups regarding the matter of this river.

When this parable is clear, God, glorified is He, has by His wisdom required that He constituted the human being, and indeed all animals, upon a nature carried by two powers: the irascible (ghadabiyyah) and the appetitive (shahwaniyyah), which is the volitional.

These two powers are what carry the character traits and attributes of the soul.

They are both embedded in the innate nature of every animal. By the power of appetite and will, it draws benefits to itself, and by the power of anger, it repels harms from itself. When it employs appetite in seeking what it needs, greed is generated from it.

When it employs anger in repelling harm from itself, courage and jealous protectiveness (ghayrah) are generated from it. If it is unable to repel that harmful thing, this produces the power of rancor.

If the arrival of what it needs is made difficult for it, and it sees another monopolizing it, this produces envy in it.

If it attains it, the intensity of its appetite and will produces the trait of stinginess and miserliness. If its greed and appetite for something become intense, and it cannot obtain it except by the irascible power, and it employs that power to obtain it, this produces in it aggression, transgression, and oppression.

From this are generated: arrogance, boastfulness, and conceit. These are traits generated from between the two powers of appetite and anger, and from the union of one with the other.

When this is clear: the river is the example of these two powers. It is poured into the channel of nature and its course toward the abodes of the heart, its cultivation, and its stores; it inevitably ruins and destroys them. The ignorant, wrongdoing souls left it in its course, so it destroyed the abodes of faith, uprooted its traces, demolished its structures, and in their place caused to grow every evil tree: of colocynth, dhari' (a thorny plant), thorns, and zaqqum. This is what the people of the Fire will eat on the Day of Return, the Day of Resurrection.

As for the pure, virtuous souls: they saw where the matter of this river would lead. So they split into three groups.

The people of spiritual exercises, struggles, seclusions, and training wanted to cut it off from its spring. But God's wisdom and what He had imprinted upon human nature refused this for them, and the natural disposition did not submit to it. So the fighting intensified, the war continued, the battle grew fierce, and the war became a matter of alternating victories and defeats.

These people directed their powers to struggling against the self to remove those traits.

Another group turned away from these (traits), occupied their souls with works, and did not respond to the calls of those traits, while leaving them in their course. However, they did not allow that river to corrupt their cultivation. Instead, they occupied themselves with fortifying the structure, making its foundation and building firm, and they saw that this river must inevitably reach it. When it reached a firm building, it did not demolish it, but took a course to the right and left of it.

These people directed the strength of their resolve and will toward construction and firming the building.

Those (the first group) directed them toward cutting off the corrupt substance from its root, out of fear of the building's destruction.

One day I asked Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, about this question: the cutting off of afflictions, and the preoccupation with purifying and cleaning the path?

He said to me, in summary of his speech: "The soul is like al-batus (a cesspit), which is a well of filth. Whenever you dig into it, it appears and comes out. But if you can cover it, pass over it, and go beyond it, then do so, and do not occupy yourself with digging into it. For you will never reach its bottom, and whenever you dig up one thing, another appears."

I said: "I asked some of the shaykhs about this matter." He said to me: "The example of the afflictions of the soul is the example of snakes and scorpions on the traveler's road. If he turns to searching the road for them and occupying himself with killing them, he will be cut off and will never be able to travel at all. Rather, let your aim be to walk, to turn away from them, and not to pay them any attention. If there appears to you among them something that hinders you from walking, then kill it, and then continue on your journey."

Shaykh al-Islam greatly approved of this and praised the one who said it.

When this is clear, then this is the third group. They saw that these traits were not created in vain or purposelessly. They are like water with which roses, thorns, fruits, and firewood are irrigated; they are like a shell and oyster shells for pearls enclosed within them. What those (the first group) feared from them is in fact the very cause of success and victory. They saw that pride is a river with which loftiness, boastfulness, insolence, oppression, and aggression are irrigated, and with which loftiness of aspiration, dignity, zeal, and defiance of God's enemies, subduing them and rising above them, are also irrigated. This (zeal) is a pearl in its oyster. So they redirected its course toward this cultivation, extracted this pearl from its shell, and left (the river) in its state within their souls, but employed it wherever its use would be most beneficial.

The Prophet ﷺ saw Abu Dujanah strutting between the two rows (in battle), and he said: "This is a walk that God dislikes, except in a place like this."

Observe how he let the course of this attribute and this trait flow in its best places.

In another hadith, which I think is in the Musnad:
"Among conceit is that which God loves, and among it is that which God hates. The conceit God loves is a man's displaying of himself in battle and at the time of charity."

Observe how a blameworthy attribute became an act of worship, and how the one who cuts off became one who connects!

As for the companion of spiritual exercises, the one who practices the path of exercises, struggles, and seclusions: far, far (is it from success)! Rather, that only leads him into afflictions, doubts, and misguidance. For the purification of souls is entrusted to the Messengers. God sent them only for this purification and entrusted it to them, and made it through their hands a call, teaching, clarification, and guidance, not a creation or inspiration. They are the ones sent to treat the souls of the nations. God, the Exalted, said:
﴿He it is who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, though before that they were in clear error﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2]

And God, the Exalted, said:
﴿Just as We sent among you a messenger from among you, reciting to you Our verses, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you did not know. So remember Me, and I will remember you; give thanks to Me and do not deny Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 151-152]

The purification of souls is more difficult and harder than the treatment of bodies. Whoever purifies his soul by exercise, struggle, and seclusion, which the Messengers did not bring, is like the sick person who treats himself by his own opinion. And where does his opinion stand relative to the knowledge of the physician? So the Messengers are the physicians of hearts. There is no way to purify and heal them except through their path, by their hands, with complete submission and surrender to them. And God is the One sought for help.

If you ask: Can character occur through acquisition, or is it something beyond acquisition?

I say: It can occur through acquisition, by cultivating and effort, until it becomes for him a natural disposition and a settled quality. The Prophet ﷺ said to al-Ashajj, the chief of 'Abd al-Qays, may God be pleased with him: "Indeed, in you are two traits that God loves: forbearance and deliberation." He said: "Are they traits I have cultivated, or did God create me upon them?" He said: "Rather, God created you upon them." He said: "Praise be to God who created me upon two traits that God and His Messenger love."

This indicates that among character there is what is natural and innate, and what is acquired. The Prophet ﷺ used to say in the opening supplication: "O God, guide me to the best of characters; none guides to the best of them except You, and turn away from me the worst of them; none turns away the worst of them except You." Thus he mentioned acquisition and divine decree. And God knows best.

[Section: The meaning of character (khuluq)]

The author of "al-Manazil" said:
"Character (khuluq) is that to which the one who makes an effort returns from his blessing."

That is: the character of every one who makes an effort is what his attributes comprise. His effort returns him to his character, as it has been said: "Indeed, cultivation (takhalluq) comes after, and the character (khuluq) is what precedes it."

Another said:
"The heart is asked to forget you, / but natures refuse the one who transfers (i.e., the one who attempts to change them)."

So the one who makes an effort toward what is not part of his description or disposition returns to his disposition, his description, and his innate nature. That to which he returns is the character.

He said: The speakers on this science have agreed that tasawwuf (Sufism, the spiritual discipline) is character. All discourse on it revolves around one pole, which is giving kindness and withholding harm.

I say: Some people make it three: withholding harm, enduring harm, and bringing comfort. Others make it two, as the Shaykh said: giving kindness and withholding harm. Others reduce it to one, which is giving kindness. All of them are correct.

He said: This possibility is only realized in three things: knowledge, generosity, and patience.

Knowledge guides him to the places of giving kindness, to distinguishing it from wrongdoing, and to placing it in its proper positions. So he does not place anger where forbearance belongs, nor the reverse; nor withholding where giving belongs, nor the reverse. Rather, he knows the places of good and evil and their ranks, and the place of every character: where to place it and where to use it well.

Generosity impels him to forgo his own rights and to insist on the rights of others. Generosity is the leader of the armies of good.

Patience preserves for him the continuation of this, and carries him to forbearance, suppressing anger, withholding harm, and not retaliating, and to every good, as has preceded. It is the greatest help in attaining every desired thing of the good of this world and the Hereafter. God, the Exalted, said:
﴿Seek help through patience and prayer; indeed, it is burdensome except for the humble﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]

These three things are what make tasawwuf attainable. Tasawwuf is one corner of the corners of true spiritual journeying (suluk), and of purification and refinement of the soul, so that it may prepare for its journey to the company of the Highest Companion and to being with the one it loves. For a person is with whom he loves. As Sumnun said: "The lovers have taken the honor of this world and the Hereafter. For a person is with whom he loves." And God knows best.

[Section: The levels of creation]

[The first level: that you know the station of creation]

He said: It is in three levels. The first level: that you know the station of creation, and that they are bound by their destinies, confined within their capacities, and held to the judgment. Through this knowledge you will benefit three things: the safety of creation from you, even from the dog; the love of creation for you; and the salvation of creation through you.

By this level is the improvement of character with creation in dealing with them and in how to associate with them.

By the second, is the improvement of character with God in one's dealings with Him.

By the third, is the level of annihilation (fana') on its foundation and root.

He says: When you know the station of creation, their measures, the operation of divine decrees upon them, that they are restricted by destiny with no escape from it whatsoever, that they are confined within their power and capacity, unable to exceed it, and that they are held to the cosmic, destined judgment without transgressing it, you will gain from this knowledge three things:

The safety of creation from you. That is: when he looks at them with the eye of reality, he does not demand of them what they cannot do, and he follows God's command to His Prophet ﷺ to accept pardon from them. Thus they are safe from his imposing upon them and obligating them to what is beyond their strength and capacity.

Also, they feel safe from his blame. In this state he excuses them for the rulings that take effect upon them concerning matters which the Sharia did not command him to enforce against them. For if they are confined within their capacity, then they should be held to account only for what one who is confined is held to account for, and be excused for what one who is confined is excused for. If there appears from them toward you any shortcoming, wrongdoing, or negligence, do not retaliate against them for it, nor contend with them; rather, forgive them for it and excuse them, in consideration of the rulings taking effect upon them, and that they are an instrument.

Here, the annihilation (al-fana', the passing away of the self in witnessing the Reality) benefits you, by witnessing the Reality rather than witnessing their offence against you, as one of the knowers ('arifin) said to a man who transgressed against him and wronged him: "If you are a wrongdoer, then the One who empowered you over me is not a wrongdoer."

[The servant's witnessings (mashahid) regarding what harm of people reaches him]

[The first witnessing: the witnessing of divine decree (qadar)]

Here the servant has eleven witnessings regarding the harm of people reaching him and their offence against him.

The first of them: the witnessing mentioned by the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, which is the witnessing of decree (qadar), and that what befalls him occurs by the will, decree and destiny of Allah. He sees it as he sees the harm of heat and cold, sickness and pain, the blowing of winds, and the cessation of rain, for all of these are brought about by the will of Allah. What Allah wills is, and its existence becomes necessary; what He does not will is not, and its existence becomes impossible. When he witnesses this, he finds rest, and knows that it is inevitably going to occur, so there is no justification for complaining about it. It is like complaining about heat, cold, sickness or death.

[Section: The second witnessing: the witnessing of patience (sabr)]

The second witnessing: the witnessing of patience, so he witnesses its obligation, its good outcome, the reward of its people, and the joy and happiness that follow from it. It frees him from the regret of retaliation and vengeance. No one has ever avenged himself without that bringing him regret. He knows that if he does not patiently endure by choice in this matter, which is praiseworthy, he will be compelled to endure something greater, which is blameworthy.

[Section: The third witnessing: the witnessing of pardon, forgiveness and forbearance]

The third witnessing: the witnessing of pardon, forgiveness and forbearance. Whenever he witnesses this, its excellence, its sweetness and its honour, he will not turn away from it except through blindness in his insight. For indeed, "Allah does not increase a servant through pardon except in honour," as is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ). This is known through experience and observation. No one has ever avenged himself without being humiliated.

Moreover, in pardon, forgiveness and forbearance there is a sweetness, tranquillity and serenity, and a nobility of the soul, its honour and its elevation above satisfying itself through vengeance, of which none is found in retaliation and revenge.

[Section: The fourth witnessing: the witnessing of contentment (rida)]

The fourth witnessing: the witnessing of contentment, which is above the witnessing of pardon and forgiveness. This only occurs for the tranquil souls, especially if the cause of what afflicts them is standing for Allah. If what he is afflicted with is for Allah, and in pursuit of His pleasure and love, then he is content with what reaches him for Allah's sake. This is the condition of every sincere lover, who is content with the hardships he encounters in pleasing the one he loves. Whenever he is resentful of it and complains about it, that is evidence of the falsehood of his love. Reality bears witness to this, and the sincere lover, as it has been said:

"For your sake I made my cheek a ground
For the mocker and the envier, until you are pleased."

Whoever is not content with what afflicts him in the path of his beloved, let him descend from the degree of love, and let him fall back, for he is not of this station.

[Section: The fifth witnessing: the witnessing of goodness (ihsan)]

The fifth witnessing: the witnessing of goodness, which is higher than what precedes it. It is that he meets the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer towards him with goodness, so that whenever the other harms him, he does good to him. What makes this easy for him is his knowledge that he has profited from him: the wrongdoer has gifted him his good deeds and erased them from his record, and recorded them in the record of the one who harmed him. Therefore it is fitting for you to thank him and to do good to him in a manner that bears no comparison to the good he has done to you.

Here it benefits to recall the question of a gift requiring recompense. This poor man has gifted you his good deeds; if you are among the people of generosity, then reward him for them, so as to confirm the gift and be safe from the donor retracting it.

There are well-known accounts of this from the people of nobility and the people of resolve.

What also makes it easy for you is your knowledge that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. If this was your conduct in response to people's harm toward you, you pardoned them and did good to them, despite your need, weakness, poverty and that. Thus does the Generous, Mighty, Self-Sufficient One deal with you in your wrongdoing: He responds to it with what you responded with towards the harm of His servant toward you. This is inevitable, and its evidence in the Sunnah is in many aspects for whoever reflects upon them.

[Section: The sixth witnessing: the witnessing of safety and coolness of heart]

The sixth witnessing: the witnessing of safety and coolness of heart. This is a very noble witnessing for whoever knows it and tastes its sweetness. It is that his heart and inner self are not occupied with the harm he has received, nor with seeking to reach the avenging of his vengeance and the healing of his soul. Rather he empties his heart of that, and sees that his safety, his coolness and his being free of it are more beneficial to him, sweeter, more pleasant, and more helpful to his interests. For when the heart becomes occupied with one thing, it misses what is more important to it and better for it, and so it is thereby defrauded. The rational person is not content with that and considers it among the actions of the foolish. Where is the safety of the heart from being filled with rancour and whisperings, and from exercising thought in pursuing revenge?

[Section: The seventh witnessing: the witnessing of security]

The seventh witnessing: the witnessing of security. For when he abandons confrontation and vengeance, he is secure from what is worse than that. And when he avenges himself, fear inevitably befalls him, for that sows enmity, and the intelligent person does not feel secure from his enemy, even if he is insignificant. How many a small person has brought down his great enemy? So when he forgives, does not avenge, and does not confront, he is secure from the generation of enmity or its increase. Without doubt, his pardon, forbearance and forgiveness break the thorn of his enemy and restrain his agitation, unlike retaliation. Reality bears witness to this as well.

[Section: The eighth witnessing: the witnessing of jihad]

The eighth witnessing: the witnessing of jihad, which is that he witnesses the harm of people toward him arising from his striving in the way of Allah, his commanding what is good, his forbidding what is evil, the establishment of the religion of Allah, and the exaltation of His words.

The person of this station: Allah has purchased from him his self, his wealth and his honour for the greatest price. If he wishes that the price be delivered to him, then let him deliver the commodity so as to deserve its price. He has no right against the one who harmed him, and nothing is owed to him before him, if he has agreed to the terms of this exchange, for his reward has become due from Allah.

This is established by the text and by the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. For this reason, "the Prophet (ﷺ) prevented the emigrants from residing in Makkah, may Allah honour it, and did not return to any of them his house or his wealth which the disbelievers had taken, nor did he make them pay the blood-money for those who were killed in the way of Allah."

When al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, resolved to make the apostates compensate for the lives and property of the Muslims that they had destroyed, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said to him, in the presence of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them: "Those are bloods and wealth that were lost in the way of Allah, and their rewards are with Allah, and there is no blood-money for a martyr." So the Companions unanimously agreed with the statement of 'Umar, and al-Siddiq agreed with it.

Whoever stands for Allah until he is harmed for Allah's sake, Allah forbids him retaliation, as Luqman said to his son: ﴿And enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil, and be patient over what afflicts you; indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Luqman: 17].

[Section: The ninth witnessing: the witnessing of blessing]

The ninth witnessing: the witnessing of blessing, and this is in several aspects.

The first: that he witnesses Allah's blessing upon him in making him one who is wronged and awaits support, rather than making him a wrongdoer who awaits abhorrence and punishment. If a rational person were given the choice between the two states, and one of them must occur, he would choose to be the one wronged.

Among them: that he witnesses Allah's blessing in the expiation of his sins through it. No believer is touched by distress, grief or harm except that Allah expiates some of his sins by it. This is in reality a remedy through which the disease of sins and transgressions is extracted. Whoever is content to meet Allah with all his ailments and sicknesses, and does not treat them in this world with a remedy that brings him healing, is defrauded and foolish. The harm of people to you is like a bitter medicine from a compassionate physician. So do not look at the bitterness and dislike of the medicine, nor at the hands it came through; rather look at the compassion of the physician who prescribed it for you, and sent it to you by the hands of one who benefited you through his harm.

Among them: that he witnesses that this trial is lighter and easier than others, for there is no tribulation except that above it is something stronger and more bitter. If there is no greater trial above it in body and wealth, then let him look at the soundness of his religion, his Islam and his monotheism, and that every affliction below the affliction of religion is easy, and that it is in reality a blessing. The true affliction is the affliction of religion.

Among them: the full payment of its reward and recompense on the Day of poverty and need. It is reported in some narrations that people will wish on the Day of Resurrection that their skins had been cut with scissors, because of what they see of the reward of the people of trial.

Moreover, the servant's joy on the Day of Resurrection will greatly increase because of the rights he has over people in wealth, life and honour. The intelligent person counts this as a treasure for the Day of poverty and need, and does not nullify it through retaliation, which benefits him nothing.

[Section: The tenth witnessing: the witnessing of the exemplar]

The tenth witnessing: the witnessing of the exemplar, which is a very noble and subtle witnessing. The intelligent and discerning person is content to have as his exemplar the messengers of Allah, His prophets, His friends, and His chosen ones among His creation. For they were the most severely tested by people, and the harm of people toward them came faster than a flood down a slope. It is sufficient to reflect upon the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, with their peoples, and the condition of our Prophet (ﷺ) and the harm of his enemies toward him, with what was not inflicted upon anyone before him. "Waraqah ibn Nawfal said to him: 'You will surely be denied, you will surely be expelled, and you will surely be harmed.' And he said to him: 'No one has come with the like of what you have come with except that he was opposed.' This continues in his heirs as it was in their predecessor (ﷺ)."

Would the servant not be content to have as his exemplar the best of Allah's creation and the special ones of His servants, the most excellent and then the most excellent?

Whoever wishes to know this, let him study the trials of the scholars and the harm of the ignorant toward them. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr composed a book on this, which he named Mihan al-'Ulama' (The Trials of the Scholars).

[Section: The eleventh witnessing: the witnessing of tawhid]

The eleventh witnessing: the witnessing of tawhid (monotheism), which is the most sublime and elevated of the witnessings. When his heart is filled with the love of Allah, sincerity toward Him and devotion to Him, preferring His pleasure, drawing near to Him, the coolness of the eye in Him, intimacy with Him, and tranquillity and repose in Him; and he takes Him as his protector to the exclusion of all others, to the extent that he entrusts all his affairs to Him, is content with Him and His decrees, and passes away in His love, fear, hope, remembrance and reliance upon Him from everything else: then there remains in his heart no room at all for witnessing people's harm to him, let alone for his heart, mind and inner self to be occupied with seeking vengeance and retaliation. This cannot occur except from a heart in which there is nothing that suffices him from that and compensates him for it. Such a heart is hungry and not satisfied; whenever it sees any food, its cravings lean toward it and its impulses are stirred toward it. But whoever's heart is filled with the highest and most excellent nourishment does not turn to what is below it. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.

(Section)

As for his saying: that he benefits by knowing the standing of people and the rulings that apply to them: their love for him and his salvation through it.

For when he deals with them in this manner, by making excuses for them, pardoning them, and abandoning confrontation with them, their dislike and love toward him become equal, and that becomes a cause of their salvation in the Hereafter as well.

...that this guides them to accept from him, and to receive most graciously what he commands them and forbids them. This is the disposition of people.

[Chapter: The Second Degree, Making Your Character Beautiful Toward the Truth]

He said: The second degree is making your character beautiful toward the Truth. Making it beautiful on your part is that you know that everything that comes from you calls for an excuse, that everything that comes from the Truth calls for thanks, and that you do not see any escape from fulfilling this.

This degree is built upon two foundations.

The first: that you know you are deficient, and everything that comes from a deficient being is deficient. It therefore necessarily requires that he apologize for it. The servant must make excuses to his Lord for everything he does, whether good or evil. As for evil, it is obvious. As for good, he apologizes for its shortcoming and does not regard it as worthy of his Lord.

So he, despite his good deeds, is apologetic for his good deeds. For this reason, Allah praised His friends for their fear of Him despite their good deeds, saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

The Prophet ﷺ said: "He is the man who fasts and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him."

When he fears this, he is more deserving of apology.

What drives him to this apology are two matters:

The first: witnessing his own shortcoming and deficiency.

The second: the sincerity of his love. The sincere lover draws near to his beloved with all his capacity. Yet he is apologetic toward him and shy before him, that he should confront him with what he has confronted him with, and he sees that his beloved's station is above him and greater than him. This is observed in the love of created beings.

The second foundation: magnifying everything that proceeds from Him, glorified is He, toward you, and acknowledging that it calls for your thanks, and that you are incapable of thanking Him for it. This is not made clear except in sincere love. For the lover considers abundant from his beloved everything he receives. If the beloved mentions him with something and gives it to him, his joy at being mentioned and at being deemed worthy of the gift is greater for him than his joy at the gift itself. Indeed, his joy at being mentioned by him overshadows his joy at the gift. And the lover is pleased by the mention of his beloved even if he receives it with something unpleasant.

As the poet said:
"Though it grieves me that you have touched me with some harm,
It gladdens me greatly that I have crossed your mind."

How much more so when the beloved bestows upon him a pleasure, however small, for he sees it only as great and momentous. So how is it with the Lord, exalted is He, who never brings anything but good? For the opposite of that is impossible concerning Him, just as the opposite of His perfection is impossible for Him. The one most knowledgeable of creation about his Lord (ﷺ) has made this clear in his saying: "And evil is not to You," meaning it is not attributed to You, is not ascribed to You, and does not proceed from You. For all His names are beautiful, all His attributes are perfection, and all His actions are bounty and justice, wisdom, mercy and benefit. So in what way could evil be ascribed to Him, glorified and exalted is He? Thus everything that proceeds from Him has praise and thanks due to Him, and in it is His blessing and grace.

His saying: "and that you do not see any escape from fulfilling this."

That is: your dealing with the Truth, glorified is He, in accordance with the requirement of apologizing for everything from you, and thanking Him for everything from Him, is a covenant with Allah, exalted is He, binding upon you forever. You do not see any escape from fulfilling it. It is not a passing matter or a state that changes. Rather, it is a binding covenant upon you to fulfill until the Day of Resurrection.

[Chapter: The Third Degree, Adorning Oneself with Purifying the Character]

He said: The third degree is adorning oneself with the purification of character, then ascending beyond the dispersion of adornment, then adorning oneself by transcending the characters.

This degree consists of three things.

The first: purifying character by completing what was mentioned in the two degrees before it. He purifies it from every impurity, turbidity and disturbance. When you do this, you ascend from its dispersion (tafriqah) to your collectedness (jam'iyyah) upon Allah. For adornment (takhalluq) and Sufism (tasawwuf) are refinement and preparation for collectedness. It was called dispersion because it is occupation with others, whereas the spiritual journey (suluk) requires full turning toward Him, and occupation with the Lord alone, apart from all else.

Then he ascends beyond that, which is transcending all characters by being absent from creation and from adornment. This absence has two levels according to them:

The first: occupation with Allah, mighty and majestic, to the exclusion of all else.

The second: annihilation (fana') in singularity (al-fardaniyyah), which they call the presence of unity (hadrat al-jam'), and it is the highest goal according to them. It is a gift bestowed, not something acquired. Yet if the servant exposes himself and is sincere in seeking, it is hoped that he will attain what he seeks. And Allah knows best.

[Chapter: The Basis of Good Character with the Truth]

The basis of good character with the Truth, and with creation, rests on two principles. Abd al-Qadir al-Kilani (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned them, saying:

"Be with the Truth without creation, and with creation without self."

So reflect: how great are these two words despite their brevity, and how comprehensive they are of the foundations of the spiritual path and of every beautiful character! The corruption of character arises only from the intervention of creation between you and Allah, exalted is He, and the intervention of the self between you and His creation. So whenever you remove creation while you are with Allah, and remove the self while you are with creation, you have attained everything that the people (al-qawm) pointed to, strove for, and circled around. And Allah is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 68, verse 6:

There has been disagreement over the construction of His words ﴿Which of you is the afflicted one﴾.

Abu 'Uthman al-Mazini said: it is a new, independent statement, and "al-maftun" is in his view a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "which of you is the affliction (fitnah)." The interrogative here concerns a matter that lies between two parties, where it is known with certainty that it does not apply to one of them, so it is fixed as applying to the other.

The majority (al-jumhur) disagree with this construction, and for them the phrase is connected to what precedes it. They then have four views on it:

The first is that the bi' (ba') is extra (za'idah), and the meaning is "which of you is the afflicted one," with the particle added to the subject, as it is added in your saying "bi-hasbika an taf'al" (it is enough for you that you do). This was stated by Abu 'Ubayd.

The second is that "al-maftun" carries the sense of "al-fitnah" (the affliction), so that the meaning is "you will see and they will see which of you is the affliction," and the ba' on this view is not extra. This was stated by al-Akhfash.

The third is that "al-maftun" is a passive participle functioning in its normal sense, but there is an omitted genitive construction, its estimated form being "which of you is the affliction of the afflicted one," and the ba' is not extra. This too was stated by al-Akhfash.

The fourth is that the ba' carries the sense of fi (in), and the estimate is "in which of the groups among you is the type that is afflicted," and the ba' on this view is locative (zarfiyyah).

All of these views are a clear artificiality (takalluf zahir), and there is no need for any of them. Rather, "satubsiru" (you will see) is here implicitly containing the sense of "tash'uru" (you will perceive) and "ta'lamu" (you will know), so it takes the ba' as one says "satash'uru bi-kadha wa-ta'lamu bihi" (you will perceive such-and-such and know of it). The Exalted said: ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ And when the wording calls you to a meaning from a nearby place, do not be amazed at one who calls you to it from a distant place.

Now, regarding the precedence of "hammaz" (one who defames) over "mashshaa' bi-namim" (one who goes about with tale-bearing): it is by rank, because walking about is subsequent to sitting in one place.

The hammaz is the one who finds fault, and that does not require movement or travelling from one's place, unlike tale-bearing (namimah).

As for the precedence of "mannaa' lil-khayr" (one who withholds good) over "mu'tadi" (transgressor): this too is by rank, because the one who withholds good begins with himself, whereas the transgressor transgresses against others, and himself before others.

A second meaning in His saying ﴿every transgressor, sinful﴾: transgression (al-'udwan) is going beyond the limit that has been set for the servant, so it is wrongdoing in measure and in attribute. Sin (al-ithm), however, is the forbidden category, and whoever engages in overstepping the limits passes on to the other category, which is sin.

A third meaning: the transgressor (al-mu'tadi) is the one who wrongs the servants of God Most High by aggression against them, while the sinner (al-atheem) is the one who wrongs himself through immorality. Placing the transgressor before the sinner here is more fitting, because it is in the context of censuring him and forbidding obedience to him. Whoever transgresses against people and wrongs them is more deserving that you should not obey him or agree with him.

There is a fourth meaning as well: he placed it before the sinner so that it would be linked to what precedes it, namely the attribute of withholding good. So He described him as one in whom there is no good for people, and that, in addition to this, he transgresses against them. Thus he comes after the withholder, for he first withholds his good and then transgresses against them second. For this reason people praise whoever brings them comfort and restrains harm from them, and this is the reality of tasawwuf (Sufism, here meaning spiritual discipline and refinement of conduct); this one brings no comfort and restrains no harm.

As for the precedence of ﴿hammaz over mashshaa' bi-namim﴾, there is another reason besides what al-[Suhayli] mentioned: his defaming is a fault for the one defamed, a belittling of him, and a display of the corruption of his state within himself.

God Most High informs us about the people of the garden whom He tested with what He tested them with in Surah (Nun) [al-Qalam]. They were a people for whom the needy had a right in their wealth: when they harvested by day, the needy would gather what fell of the dates. They wanted to harvest at night so that this right would lapse and no needy person would come to them. So He punished them: He sent upon their garden a calamity (ṭā'if) while they slept, and it became like the harvested-black (al-ṣarīm).

This was because they devised a stratagem to cancel the share of the needy by harvesting it in the early morning, before the needy came.

So in this there is a lesson for everyone who schemes to cancel a right, whether one of the rights of God Most High or the rights of His servants.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 68, verses 35–36:

Glory be to Him, He rebuked those who equated the Muslims with the criminals, and the obedient with the corrupters, even though all of them fall under the universal will (al-mashi'ah al-kawniyyah) and the general decree.

He also said in Tariq al-hijratayn (The Path of the Two Migrations):

He denounced their judgment in this matter and presented it in the form of rebuke, not of statement, so as to alert minds to this, since it is something that natural disposition rejects and sound reason refuses. And the Exalted said: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of the Garden are not equal; the companions of the Garden, they are the triumphant﴾ [al-Hashr: 20]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Are those who know and those who do not know alike? Only the people of understanding take heed﴾ [az-Zumar: 9].

Rather, a single created thing does not have its upper parts equal to its lower parts; its back is not like its front, nor its head like its feet, and neither is fit for what the other is fit for. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created the good and the bad, the easy and the difficult, the harmful and the beneficial. And these are the components of the earth: some of it is fit to be a polish for the eye, and some of it is fit for the kiln and the fire.

By this and the like, the perfection of power and the perfection of wisdom are known. The perfection of power lies in creating opposites, and the perfection of wisdom lies in placing each thing in its proper rank and position. The knowledgeable person is one who does not set up a conflict between the power of Allah and His wisdom: if he affirms the power while denying the wisdom, he has impugned wisdom and nullified it; and if he affirms the wisdom while denying the power, he has impugned power and diminished it. Rather, he links power with wisdom, and knows that both encompass all that Allah has created and will create. Just as nothing occurs except by His power and will, so nothing occurs except by His wisdom. And since the human intellects have no way to comprehend this in detail, it suffices them to believe in what they know and witness of it, then they infer the unseen from the seen and reason from what they know to what they do not know.

(Admonition)

How can one be granted a good end when Allah, glorified is He, has left his heart heedless of His remembrance, follows his desire, and his affair has been neglected (Qur'an 18:28)? Far is the one whose heart is far from Allah, the Exalted, heedless of Him, a slave to his desire, a captive of his lusts, whose tongue is dry from His remembrance, and whose limbs are idle from obedience to Him and busy with disobedience—far is he from being granted a good end.

The fear of the end has broken the backs of the God-fearing, while the wrongdoing evildoers behave as though they had obtained a written guarantee of safety. ﴿Or do you have oaths binding upon Us until the Day of Resurrection, that yours is what you will judge? Ask them which of them will stand surety for that.﴾

As it has been said:

O you who feel secure from the foul deeds you commit, has there come to you a decree of safety that you yourself possess?

You have combined two things: security and following desire. This, and one of them destroys a person.

The doers of good have traveled the path of fears, and that is a path you do not tread.

You neglected sowing at the time of planting, out of folly, so how will you reap when people harvest?

Yet the most astonishing thing about you is your renunciation of the abode of permanence for a life you will surely leave behind.

Who, then, is the fool—you before Allah, or the one defrauded in a sale, whose loss will catch up with him?
